# SK1120 — A reflection call asks what `is` answers

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

`typeof(T).IsInstanceOfType(x)` and `typeof(T).IsAssignableFrom(x.GetType())` both spell `x is T` as a `Type` load and a virtual call.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Modernization |
| Default severity | suggestion |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | yes, review it |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 2.0 |
| Supersedes | CanSimplifyIsAssignableFrom |

## Why

The `is` operator is one IL instruction, and more to the point it is the spelling every C# reader recognises and the one that composes with a pattern — `x is T t` binds the value that the reflection call would need a separate, unchecked cast for. ⚠ **Nothing in the shipped toolchain reports either shape**, measured rather than assumed: compiled at `AnalysisMode=All`, `AnalysisLevel=latest-all` and `EnforceCodeStyleInBuild=true`, with the whole `Style` and `CodeQuality` categories raised to `warning`, both shapes produce no `IDE*` and no `CA*` diagnostic. ⚠ **The instrument was verified in the same build rather than trusted**: planted shapes produce `IDE0059` and `IDE0090`, so the zero beside them is a zero from clean analysis and not from analysis that never ran — and at the default `EnforceCodeStyleInBuild=true` alone, *no* `IDE*` rule appears at all, because they ship enabled and `Hidden`.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
if (typeof(Stream).IsInstanceOfType(source)) {
    Copy(source);
}

if (typeof(Stream).IsAssignableFrom(source.GetType())) {
    Copy(source);
}
```

Write:

```csharp
if (source is Stream) {
    Copy(source);
}

if (source is Stream) {
    Copy(source);
}
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **The two shapes are one concept and they are not equally safe, which is why the rule ships `fixIsSafe: false` although one half of it is exactly total.** Fourteen shapes were compiled and run for `IsInstanceOfType` — `null`, a boxed value type, a non-null and a null `int?`, an interface, a covariant interface, array covariance, an array through `IList<T>`, an enum boxed as itself and as its underlying `int`, and a wrong type — and the reflection call and the operator agree on **every one**. `IsAssignableFrom(x.GetType())` agrees on six of the same shapes and **diverges on the seventh**: `x.GetType()` throws `NullReferenceException` where `x is T` is `false`. A rule carries one safety answer and the pair takes the weaker one. ⚠ **The nullable-value-type divergence this rule was expected to have does not exist, and the expectation is refuted.** `Type.IsAssignableFrom` documents — and the probe confirms — a special case for a nullable value type and its underlying type: `typeof(int?).IsAssignableFrom(typeof(int))` is `true`, and `(object)someInt is int?` is `true` as well, so the two agree. ⚠ **Three types make `typeof(T)` compile and `x is T` not compile**, all three confirmed against the compiler rather than assumed: a **static class**, a **`ref struct`**, and an **unbound generic** such as `typeof(List<>)`. Each is a legal reflection call and an uncompilable pattern, and each is declined; `void`, a pointer, a function pointer and an error type are declined for the same reason. ⚠ **`typeof(A).IsAssignableFrom(typeof(B))` is never reported**, declined by construction rather than by a name list: the argument is required to be a `GetType()` call, and a question about two types with no value in it has no `is` spelling at all. ⚠ **`SK2181`'s shape is handed over by the BCL rather than by a guard, and the guard written for it was removed as unreachable.** `System.Type` declares its own `public new Type GetType()`, so `t.GetType()` on a `Type` receiver binds to `System.Type.GetType()` and never to `object.GetType()` — asked directly, the model answers `System.Type.GetType()` with containing type `System.Type`. Requiring the `GetType()` to be `object`'s therefore already declines every expression `SK2181` owns, and removing the explicit handover turned no fixture red because there was nothing left for it to do. ⚠ **The operand must be a reference type.** `int n; n is object` is CS0183, "the given expression is always of the provided type" — a warning the fix would introduce, which the fixture harness' re-binding test correctly treats as a broken fix. A value operand boxes into the reflection call and is a different, rarer shape; it is declined rather than reported without a usable edit. ⚠ **CS8121**: a target type that no conversion reaches from the operand's type is declined through `ClassifyConversion`, because the reflection call is legal there and always false while the pattern does not compile at all. ⚠ **The operand must be a primary expression**, because the rewrite moves it from an argument position, where every precedence is legal, to the left of a relational operator, where most are not — `a ? b : c is T` does not mean `(a ? b : c) is T`. ⚠ **The replacement is parenthesised wherever the call was an operand of an expression**: `!typeof(T).IsInstanceOfType(x)` becomes `!(x is T)`, and without the parentheses it parses as `(!x) is T` and does not compile. ⚠ The type is re-spelled from the `typeof` operand's own source text rather than from the symbol, so the edit needs no `using` the file does not have and no qualification the file does not use. A comment or a preprocessor directive inside the replaced span withdraws the finding. Generated code is excluded. ⚠ **The rule is reported inside an expression tree, and the belief that it must not be is refuted.** "An expression tree may not contain an `is` pattern" (CS8122) is about the *pattern* forms — a constant pattern, a declaration pattern, a recursive pattern — and this rule emits none of them: `x is T` with no designation is the type-test **operator**, `ExpressionType.TypeIs`, which expression trees have represented since LINQ shipped. Eleven emitted shapes were compiled inside an `Expression<Func<object, bool>>` — a reference type, an interface, a negated test, a value type, `int?`, an array, a constructed generic, an enum, an unconstrained type parameter, and the same test inside a delegate lambda nested in the tree — and every one compiles. Withholding them would have been ten false negatives. ⚠ **One `typeof` operand is the exception, and it is the tuple type**: the type is re-spelled from source text, so `typeof((int, int))` emits `x is (int, int)`, which the parser reads as a pattern rather than a type test and which really is CS8122 inside a tree. That spelling alone is declined there, and only there — outside an expression tree it compiles and asks the identical question, so the finding stands. `typeof(ValueTuple<int, int>)` is the same type and is reported everywhere, which is why the test is on the syntax rather than on the symbol.
